---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:motzkin}
    The number of $2$-stack-sortable permutations in $S_n'$ is the $n$th Motzkin number $M_n$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
The hook-length of $1$ in the tableau below is $6$, as shown below.
\[\begin{ytableau}11 & 9 & 5 \\ *(Salmon) 10 & *(Salmon) 7 \\ *(Salmon) 8 \\ *(Salmon) 6 & *(Salmon) 3 & *(Salmon) 2 & *(Apricot) 1 \\ 4 \end{ytableau}\]
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{pro:theory}
    There exists a map $\theta$ from $S_n'$ to $\mathcal T_n$ such that
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the preimage of every $T \in \mathcal T_n$ has $\prod_ch(c)$ elements, where the product is taken over all cells $c$ not in the first column of $T$, and
        \item for all $\pi \in S_n'$, the width of $\theta(\pi)$ is the stack-sorting depth of $\pi$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:final-element}
    The set $\widetilde S_n$ is closed under $s$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $\pi \in \widetilde S_n$. We need to show the part of $s(\pi)$ after $0$ is increasing. Consider the moment immediately after $0$ is popped from the stack when $s$ is applied on $\pi$. Let the remainder of the input permutation be $r = (r_1,\dots,r_i)$ and the elements of the stack from top to bottom be $s = (s_1,\dots,s_j)$. Now $r$ and $s$ are both increasing. If $s_1 < r_1$, then $s_1$ is popped. Otherwise, $s_1 > r_1$, so $r_1$ is pushed in, then immediately popped. In either case, the least element of $r$ and $s$ is added to the end of the output permutation. Iterating $i + j$ times moves the elements of $r$ and $s$ to the end of $s(\pi)$ in increasing order.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
For the permutation $\mathbf{8395714260} \in S_9'$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \rho_1 &= \mathbf{83\textcolor{red}95\textcolor{red}7142\textcolor{red}6} \\
        \rho_2 &= \mathbf{3\textcolor{red}8\textcolor{red}512\textcolor{red}4} \\
        \rho_3 &= \mathbf{\textcolor{red}31\textcolor{red}2} \\
        \rho_4 &= \mathbf{\textcolor{red}1} \\
        \rho_5 &= \varepsilon,
    \end{align*}
    where the red elements of $\rho_i$ are the elements of $M(\rho_i)$. Then $T_\pi$ is the following.
    \[\begin{ytableau}
        9 & 8 & 3 \\
        7 & 5 \\
        6 & 4 & 2 & 1
    \end{ytableau}\]
    The tableau $T_\pi$ contains each element of $\{1,\dots,9\}$ exactly once. Also, $T_\pi$ is antistandard and has width $4 = \langle \pi\rangle$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:first}
    $\lvert W'_2(n)\rvert = \lvert X_n'\rvert$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:second}
    $\lvert X_n'\rvert = \lvert X_n\rvert$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:third}
    $\lvert X_n\rvert = \lvert Y_n\rvert$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We claim the map $\theta$ of Proposition \ref{pro:theory} is a bijection from $W_2'(n)$ to $X_n'$. By the second part of Proposition \ref{pro:theory}, if $\pi \in W_2'(n)$, then $\theta(\pi)$ is an antistandard composition tableau with $n$ cells and at most $2$ columns. Also, the hook-length of every cell $c$ in the second column of $\theta(\pi)$ is $1$, since the unique cell that is strictly left of $c$, weakly above $c$, and strictly below $\operatorname{up}(\operatorname{left}(c))$ is the cell immediately to the left of $c$. Therefore, the first part of Proposition \ref{pro:theory} implies the preimage of every $T \in X_n'$ consists of exactly one element. Hence $\theta: W_2'(n) \to X_n'$ is a bijection and $\lvert W_2'(n)\rvert = \lvert X_n'\rvert$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The map replacing each entry $c$ with $n + 1 - c$ is an involution on the set of tableaux sending $X_n'$ to $X_n$, hence $\lvert X_n'\rvert = \lvert X_n\rvert$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{exa:f}
    We apply $f$ three times on the tableau below in sequence, where we use cases (a), (b), and (a) of $f$, in that order. The overhangs are highlighted in green.
    \[\begin{ytableau}
    1 \\ *(LimeGreen) 2 & *(LimeGreen) 5 \\ 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 \\ 6 \\ 7 & 11 \\ 10 \\ 12 & 13
    \end{ytableau} \quad \xrightarrow f \quad \begin{ytableau}
    1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 \\ 6 \\ *(LimeGreen) 7 & *(LimeGreen) 11 \\ 10 \\ 12 & 13
    \end{ytableau} \quad \xrightarrow f \quad \begin{ytableau}
    1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 7 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 \\ 6 & 11 \\ 10 \\ *(LimeGreen) 12 & *(LimeGreen) 13
    \end{ytableau} \quad \xrightarrow f \quad \begin{ytableau}
    1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 7 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 & 13 \\ 6 & 11 \\ 10 & 12
    \end{ytableau}\]
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{exa:g}
    We apply $g$ three times on the tableau below in sequence, where we use cases (a), (c), and (b) of $g$, in that order.
    \[\begin{ytableau}
    1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 7 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 & 13 \\ 6 & 11 \\ 10 & 12
    \end{ytableau} \quad \xrightarrow g \quad \begin{ytableau}
    1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 7 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 \\ 6 & 11 \\ 10 \\ 12 & 13
    \end{ytableau} \quad \xrightarrow g \quad \begin{ytableau}
    1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 \\ 6 \\ 7 & 11 \\ 10 \\ 12 & 13
    \end{ytableau} \quad \xrightarrow g \quad \begin{ytableau}
    1 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 9 \\ 6 \\ 7 & 11 \\ 10 \\ 12 & 13
    \end{ytableau}\]
    Note that this is exactly the reverse of the sequence in Example \ref{exa:f}. This holds since $f$ and $g$ are inverses, which we will show in Lemma \ref{lem:inverses}.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:inverses}
    The maps $f$ and $g$ are inverses.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We need to show $f \circ g = g \circ f = \operatorname{id}$. We first show $f \circ g = \operatorname{id}$. Let $T \in Z_n \setminus X_n$. Let $F = f(T)$ and $G = g(T)$. We work via cases of $g$.
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item Case (a). Then $i(G) = d_2(T)$ and $j(G) = c_3(T)$. Then case (a) of $f$ reverses the application of $g$ to $T$.
        \item Case (b). Similar to case (a), but $i(G) = c_2(T)$ instead of $d_2(T)$. Case (a) of $f$ reverses the application of $g$ to $T$ again.
        \item Case (c). Then $i(G) = c_2(T)$, $j(G) = c_2'(T)$, and $i'(G) = c_3(T)$. Since $i'(G) < j(G)$, case (b) of $f$ reverses the application of $g$ to $T$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Now we show $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}$. Let $T \in Z_n \setminus Y_n$. We work via cases of $f$.
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item Case (a). Suppose there is exactly one $1$-cell row above the overhang of $T$, and the row immediately below the overhang of $T$ has $2$ cells. Then $c_1(F)$ is the cell above $i(T)$ in $T$, $c_2(F) = i(T)$, and $c_3(F) = j(T)$. Hence $c_1$ and $c_2$ are in the same row, and applying case (b) of $g$ reverses the application of $f$ to $T$. Otherwise, $d_2(F) = i(T)$ and $c_3(F) = j(T)$, and case (a) of $g$ reverses the application of $f$ to $T$.
        \item Case (b). Then $c_3(F) = i'(T)$, $c_2(F) = i(T)$, $c_1(F)$ is the cell immediately above $i$ in $T$, and $c_2'(F) = j(T)$. Now case (c) of $g$ reverses the application of $f$ to $T$. \qedhere
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The well-defined maps $f: Z_n \setminus Y_n \to Z_n \setminus X_n$ and $g: Z_n \setminus X_n \to Z_n \setminus Y_n$ satisfy $f \circ g = g \circ f = \operatorname{id}$, hence they are bijections. Hence $\lvert Z_n \setminus X_n\rvert = \lvert Z_n \setminus Y_n\rvert$. As $X_n,Y_n \subseteq Z_n$, this implies $\lvert Z_n\rvert - \lvert X_n\rvert = \lvert Z_n\rvert - \lvert Y_n\rvert$, or $\lvert X_n\rvert = \lvert Y_n\rvert$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark--1: body_md -->
Let $g': Y_n \to X_n$ be defined by $g'(T) = g^{k_T}(T)$ for all $T$, where $k_T$ is the number of cells in the third column of $T$. Each application of $g$ decreases the number of cells in the third column by $1$, so $g'$ is well-defined. Similarly, let $f': X_n \to Y_n$ be the map sending $T$ to the tableaux obtained by repeatedly applying $f$ to $T$ until the result lies in $Y_n$. This process terminates, since each application increases the number of cells in the third column. As $f$ and $g$ are inverses, $f'$ and $g'$ are inverses and hence bijections. Therefore, $f'$ and $g'$ are explicit bijections between $X_n$ and $Y_n$.
<!-- end remark--1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
\[\lvert W_2'(n)\rvert \stackrel{\ref{lem:first}}= \lvert X'_n\rvert \stackrel{\ref{lem:second}}= \lvert X_n\rvert \stackrel{\ref{thm:third}}= \lvert Y_n\rvert \stackrel{\text{\cite{motzkinsyt}}}= M_n. \qedhere\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
